    <title>Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:50:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23211v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23211v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23208v1</id>
    <title>Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:49:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23208v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23208v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23207v1</id>
    <title>Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:48:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23207v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23207v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.</summary>

    <title>Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:48:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23206v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23206v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.</summary>

    <title>Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:44:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23202v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23202v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-17T18:38:28Z</updated>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23198v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.</summary>

    <summary>Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual</summary>

    <summary>Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved.     <summary>THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature.     <title>WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:35:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23192v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23192v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed.
  We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.</summary>

    <title>Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:33:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23189v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23189v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human operators. Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of segmentation targets. We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases. The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities, branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks, so the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, using nine refinement configurations and seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy, and remains an open research direction. Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative to anatomy-specific correction models. Code: https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace</summary>

    <title>Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:32:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23188v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23188v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.</summary>

    <title>Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:30:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23186v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23186v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.</summary>

    <title>Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:24:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23179v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23179v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.</summary>

    <title>Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:23:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23177v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23177v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.</summary>

    <title>Inference after coding agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:22:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23174v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23174v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.</summary>

    <title>Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:17:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23165v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23165v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.</summary>

    <title>Attribution Through the Decoder: Prediction-Space Explanations for Structured Outputs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:13:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23161v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23161v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Networks that predict angles, gaze directions, and rotations do not output these quantities directly: they emit raw coordinates that a fixed decoder, such as normalization, maps to the final prediction. Attribution methods are usually applied to the raw coordinates, so they can credit inputs for changes the decoder discards, such as rescaling a vector when only its direction matters. The resulting explanation can highlight inputs that have no effect on the prediction. We instead attribute through the decoder differential, which for normalization decoders reduces to a scaled tangent projection. We characterize invariance to output rescaling, show that every fixed smooth scalar target on a sphere has points of zero tangential sensitivity, and show that an endpoint-projected variant of Integrated Gradients can still attribute to scale-only inputs, whereas direct angular Integrated Gradients cannot. On synthetic tasks with analytically known relevance, ambient attribution assigns up to 72% of its mass to an irrelevant region. On MPIIGaze validation data, tangent Grad-CAM produces 44% greater prediction displacement under 10% pixel deletion. On PASCAL3D+ with a 6D rotation decoder, the full differential improves mean deletion displacement by 14.1 degrees over the ambient coordinate sum and by 13.8 degrees over a decoder-invariant scalar. Results for a two-polarity tangent LayerCAM variant are mixed: it exceeds ambient-sum LayerCAM on circular regression but no difference is detected on quaternion pose. These results separate two failure sources, radial contamination and scalarization loss. The approach uses existing attribution methods with decoder-aware targets, although some variants also require changes to attribution aggregation. An invariant attribution can still miss inputs that drive the prediction, so invariance and deletion performance should each be checked.</summary>

    <summary>Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model using 200 unique languages in more than 9{,}000 evaluation settings. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.</summary>

    <title>Quantum simulation of neutral-meson mixing and decay on a reprogrammable photonic processor</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:10:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23156v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23156v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neutral mesons oscillate into their antiparticles while decaying, so their dynamics is generated by a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian which a quantum simulator restricted to unitary operations cannot implement directly. We propose a reprogrammable photonic processor that simulates this open-system evolution through dilation and analyze it at the circuit level. The effective Hamiltonian is reconstructed exactly from measured lifetimes, mass and width differences, and the CP-violation parameter $|q/p|$. Through a singular-value decomposition and a single ancilla that encodes the total decay probability, its propagator is embedded in a four-mode unitary, which is compiled at each time step into a rectangular interferometer on a hexagonal mesh of tunable Mach-Zehnder units. Circuit simulations including coupler, propagation, and bend losses show that one fixed device, reprogrammed only through its control voltages, reproduces the flavor oscillation and decay of neutral kaons and of $B_d$ and $B_s$ mesons, with $x=Δm/Γ$ from 0.77 to 26.9. Over 500 time steps per system, the mean fidelity lies between 0.99979 and 0.99982, and no step falls below 0.9996. Because every optical path crosses nine tunable units, uniform insertion loss reduces only the transmitted power, whereas unit-to-unit loss variations lower the fidelity quadratically, $1-\langle F\rangle \simeq 0.08σ^2$ for a loss standard deviation $σ$ in dB. A leading-order analysis traces this coefficient to the routing of light through the mesh, reproduces the fitted value to within 2%, and explains why it is the same for all three mesons; a mean fidelity of 0.999 tolerates $σ\approx 0.11$ dB. The ancillary outputs encode the total decay probability without postselection, and the reported probabilities are normalized to the collected optical power.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23154v1</id>
    <title>Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:06:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23154v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23154v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23149v1</id>
    <title>Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:03:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23149v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23149v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23142v1</id>
    <title>Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:59:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23142v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23142v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.</summary>

    <title>RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:55:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23138v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23138v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.</summary>

    <title>Correcting Flows with Marginal Matching</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:53:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23134v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23134v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Flow matching models, ODE-based generative models, generate samples by gradually morphing a simple source distribution into a target distribution. However, these models still face challenges in optimally balancing computational efficiency with generation fidelity. While predictor-corrector schemes have been proven to help address this issue in diffusion models effectively, their application to flow matching models remains under-explored. In this work we present a novel training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching, which exploits the fact that the ODE can be easily reversed. Our key idea, termed Marginal Matching, is to correct samples at a particular time step in the forward ODE towards a matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE. This scheme proves to reduce a bound on the distance between the data distribution and the learned distribution, motivating two different implementations for the correction function. We show that our proposed method improves sample quality on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, with minimal overhead in computation time.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23132v1</id>
    <title>Non-equilibrium topological order from Floquet anyon proliferation in the toric code</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:50:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23132v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23132v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We analyze the dynamics of Kitaev's toric code in Floquet quenches where the drive coherently creates and propagates fermionic $f$ anyons. We show that the long-time state departs from pure-state topological order but retains long-range entanglement, thereby realizing a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order. As a key result enabling this analysis, we derive decompositions of the entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity that separate the ground-state value, including topological terms, from a contribution given by the driven quasiparticles. For a drive inducing non-interacting $f$ dynamics, these decompositions allow us to leverage numerical methods for free fermions and to link the emergence of the proposed long-time ordered state to the equilibration of $f$ anyons to a periodic Gibbs ensemble. For drives inducing Floquet eigenstate thermalization of $f$, our results suggest a scenario where Floquet heating of the $f$ sector stabilizes a genuine non-equilibrium topological phase, in contrast with the usual view of heating as an obstacle to order in periodically driven systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23130v1</id>
    <title>A Neural Envelope Method for Rapid Gradient-based Optimum Takeoff Trajectory Design</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:47:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23130v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23130v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Urban air mobility arises to mitigate ground traffic congestion. Multidisciplinary analysis and optimization (MDAO) has been introduced to reduce the energy consumption, thereby expanding aircraft performance. Surrogate-based MDAO lowers the cost of optimization, but multimodality disrupts global optimum search for both simulation-based and surrogate-based optimizations. Convex envelopes convert multimodal spaces into unimodal spaces, permitting efficient convex optimization; however, convexifying a design space may produce infeasible "optimal" designs due to complex design constraints. To address these challenges, this work proposes the coupling of a physics-constrained generative adversarial networks (physicsGAN) and neural envelope to transform original, constrained, non-convex optimizations into unconstrained, convex optimizations. Specifically, the physicsGAN discovers a feasible design space where all design candidates inherently satisfy all constraints, by penalizing surrogate-predicted constraint violations during training. Moreover, the neural envelope constructs a neural network-based convex envelope for the transformed objective function within the physicsGAN-discovered feasible space. Note that the neural envelope only needs to deal with objective function since constraints are inherently satisfied in the feasible space. The neural envelope is demonstrated on takeoff trajectory optimizations of the Airbus A3 Vahana eVTOL aircraft. Results show that neural envelopes achieve a 99.91% mean accuracy within a flight-condition space compared with reference convex envelopes. Neural-envelope-enabled optimizations achieve 99.84% accuracy on the global optimum design, costing only 0.04 seconds on average. The neural envelope accelerates the trajectory optimization by 53 and 162 times on average compared to the physicsGAN-enabled gradient-based and global optimizations, respectively.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23129v1</id>
    <title>Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:46:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23129v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23129v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Advection-diffusion priors are a common way to make neural sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts physics-informed. We test where such a prior must enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM to help, using daily NOAA OISST v2.1 for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark on the same grid with known currents of controlled strength. (i) On real data, a soft advection-diffusion residual with a learned velocity gives no reliable benefit (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 degrees C, 95% interval [-0.022, +0.008]); a plain temporal-smoothness penalty matches it, and equivalence within 3% is not established either. (ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. (iii) Supplied currents help on synthetic data, but mostly as information: giving them to the network as input channels, without transport, recovers 92% of the transport design's lead-5 gain, and a frozen-current numerical forecast does as well as either. (iv) With GLORYS12 reanalysis currents on real data, the transport design is 6% and 4% worse at leads 1 and 5; reanalysis advection explains essentially none of the daily OISST change (correlation 0.02), and frozen-current transport is worse than persistence. (v) The defect that matters is lead-dependent miscalibration shared by every model. One variance multiplier per lead, fitted on validation data, brings 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 at all leads and lowers day-1 CRPS by 13-21%; fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts fixes long-lead coverage but costs short-lead skill. This version withdraws an earlier claim of an 81% CRPS reduction that came from an uncontrolled comparison.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23128v1</id>
    <title>Causality, determinism and predictability: Probing nature through classical and quantum eyes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:45:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23128v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23128v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this article, mainly focussed on students and interested readers, we discuss how the understanding of causality, determinism and predictability is transformed as we move from the classical world view to the quantum description. We first explain how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outline the notion of causality. A paradigm shift occurs within the framework of quantum mechanics where we have to revisit, and even give up, the notions of determinism, predictability and maybe even strict causality. An engrossing and fascinating debate ensues, after the formulation of quantum mechanics among the giants of physics like Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and many others. While some questions have been settled in the last century in favour of quantum world view, there are still many open questions, most important of which is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.</summary>

   * Patients with a history of colorectal cancer treatment by surgical resection who develop radiological or clinical evidence of metastatic cancer do not require separate histological or cytological confirmation of metastatic disease unless:

     * Either an interval of greater than five years has elapsed between the primary surgery and the development of metastatic disease OR
     * The primary cancer was stage I.
   * Clinicians should consider biopsy of lesions to establish the diagnosis of metastatic colorectal cancer in each case if there is substantial clinical ambiguity regarding the nature or source of apparent metastases.
2. No prior treatment for advanced or metastatic colorectal cancer

   * Patients may have received prior adjuvant chemotherapy (no more than 6 months or 4 cycles) or radiation with radiosensitizing chemotherapy. The last course of chemotherapy must have concluded \> 12 months prior to registration. Patients may not have previously received irinotecan ≤ or oxaliplatin therapy in either the adjuvant or metastatic setting. No concurrent use of additional investigational agents is allowed while participating in this study.
3. Patients may not have had prior radiotherapy to greater than 25% of bone marrow.

   Standard adjuvant rectal cancer chemoradiation will not exclude the patient from protocol entry. Radiation must have concluded ≥ 4 weeks from registration.
4. Patients should have completed any major surgery ≥ 4 weeks from registration. Patients must have completed any minor surgery ≥ 2 weeks from registration. Patients must have fully recovered from the procedure. Insertion of a vascular access device is not considered major or minor surgery.
5. No previous or concurrent malignancy is allowed except for adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, in situ cervical cancer, or other cancer for which the patient has been disease-free for five years.
6. Age ≥ 18 years
7. CTC (ECOG) performance status of 0-1.
8. No evidence of Gilbert's syndrome - Patients with Gilbert's Syndrome may have a greater risk of irinotecan toxicity due to the abnormal glucuronidation of SN-38. Evidence of Gilbert's Syndrome would include a prior finding of an isolated elevation of indirect bilirubin.
9. Patients must have at least one paraffin block available or appropriate number of unstained slides for analysis of EGFR status.
10. No symptomatic sensory peripheral neuropathy of ≥ grade II at baseline.
11. Non-pregnant and non-lactating

    * Women of child bearing potential (WOCBP) must have a negative serum or urine pregnancy test (minimum sensitivity 25 IU/L or equivalent units of HCG within 72 hours prior to initiation of treatment. This is because DNA alkylating agents are known to be teratogenic, and the effects of irinotecan, OXAL, 5-FU and C225 on a developing fetus at the recommended therapeutic doses are unknown.
    * Women of child bearing potential includes:

      * any female who has experienced menarche and who has not undergone surgical sterilization (hysterectomy, bilateral tubal ligation or bilateral oophorectomy) or
      * is not postmenopausal \[defined as amenorrhea ≥ 12 consecutive months\] or
      * women on hormone replacement therapy \[HRT\] with documented serum follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) level \> 35 mIU/mL
      * women who are using oral, implanted or injectable contraceptive hormones or mechanical products such as an intrauterine device or barrier methods (diaphragm, condoms, spermicides) to prevent pregnancy or practicing abstinence or where partner is sterile (eg, vasectomy), should be considered to be of child bearing potential.
    * Should a woman become pregnant or suspect she is pregnant while participating on on this study, she should inform her physician immediately. Because the risk of toxicity of these agents in nursing infants is also unknown, breastfeeding should be discontinued.
12. No known central nervous system metastases or carcinomatous meningitis.
13. No interstitial pneumonia or extensive and symptomatic interstitial fibrosis of the lung.
14. No pleural effusion or ascites that causes ≥ grade 2 dyspnea.
15. No predisposing colonic or small bowel disorders in which the symptoms are uncontrolled as indicated by baseline pattern of \> 3 watery or soft stools daily in patients without a colostomy or ileostomy. Patients with a colostomy or ileostomy may be entered at investigator discretion.
16. No prior exposure or known sensitivity to chimerized or murine antibodies, C225 (or other EGFR inhibitors) or any tyrosine kinase inhibitors
17. No significant history of cardiac disease, such as unstable angina, CHF, MI, stroke or a LVEF below the institutional range of normal on a baseline multiple gated acquisition (MUGA) or echocardiogram.
18. Patients must not have an uncontrolled seizure disorder, or active neurological disease.
19. Patients may not have received itraconazole or ketoconazole less than 4 weeks prior to registration.
20. Required Initial Laboratory Values:

    * Granulocytes ≥ 1500/ µl
    * Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 gram/dL (patient may be transfused to meet this criterion)
    * Platelet count ≥ 100,000/ µl
    * Creatinine ≤ 1.5 x Upper limits of normal (ULN)

1. Signed and dated written Informed Consent Form (ICF) in accordance with ICH-GCP and local legislation prior to admission to the trial.

3. Patients must have histologically or cytologically documented surgically unresectable locally-advanced or metastatic Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal (SCCA).
4. Patients with loco-regional anal cancer as initial diagnosis must have unresectable progressive locally advanced or metastatic SCCA after failure of at least one line (but not more than two lines) of previous systemic treatment unless ineligible for or intolerant to this systemic therapy.

   Patients with metastatic anal cancer as initial diagnosis (no prior treatment for loco-regional cancer) must have failed one line of previous systemic treatment (chemotherapy ± radiotherapy) for the metastatic anal cancer unless ineligible for or intolerant to this systemic treatment. The ocular surface is a unique mucosal immune compartment in which immunological features act in concert to foster a tolerant microenvironment (immune privilege). The corneal epithelial barrier is the first line of defense that forms a protective barrier against pathogens, pollutants, and allergens. The ocular microbiota has a role in maintaining the homeostasis of the ocular surface and preservation of barrier function. Vitamin D functions as enforcing intercellular junctions and maintaining intestinal epithelial barrier integrity; metabolites from the gut microbiota may also regulate expression of vitamin D receptor (VDR). Low serum vitamin D levels have been shown to predispose to a variety of allergic disorders. A recent study shows that corneas contain vitamin D and VDR; vitamin D enhances corneal epithelial barrier function. However, research data of the role of vitamin D in ocular microenvironment of AC are insufficient and controversial. In recent research, the investigators found allergic inflammation of ocular surface weakened corneal epithelial barrier, modulated the signal pathway of retinal pigment epithelial cells, and enhanced scleral tissue remodeling, resulting in myopia in progression. However, there are few studies available to investigate the role of vitamin D in ocular surface microenvironment, ocular inflammation, and visual acuity in AC. Moreover, understanding the interaction of vitamin D, ocular microbiota, and ocular inflammation may provide a new target for the development of therapeutic interventions of ocular allergy and restore visual function."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Allergic Conjunctivitis"],"keywords":["allergic conjunctivitis, immune privilege","corneal epithelial barrier","microbiota","vitamin D","ocular Patients must have:

Exclusion Criteria

Co-existing Condition:

Patients with the following symptoms or conditions are excluded:

* Leukemia or lymphoma.
* Current gastrointestinal bleeding by stool guaiac.
* Extensive bone metastases or significant radiographic osteoporosis in patients with solid tumors.
* Active heart disease such as uncontrolled angina, uncompensated congestive heart failure, or dysrhythmias requiring antiarrhythmics.
* Acute intercurrent infection other than genital herpes.
* Symptomatic or known central nervous system involvement (including brain metastases) unless stable and off therapy.

Concurrent Medication:

Excluded:

* Other anticancer therapy.
* Other investigational agents.

Patients with the following prior conditions are excluded:

* History of acute or chronic gastrointestinal bleeding or inflammatory bowel disease.
* History of myocardial infarction within past 6 months.

Excluded:

* Anticancer therapy within the past 3 weeks (6 weeks for nitrosourea or mitomycin C).

Patients with one of the following indications:

Phase I:

HR+/HER2- aBC with disease progression on or following at least one line of hormone-based therapy in combination with a CDK4/6i and at least one additional line of systemic therapy for metastatic disease.

Histologically and/or cytologically confirmed diagnosis of locally advanced or metastatic cancer with a CCNE1 amplification. For dose expansion only: no more than 3 prior lines of therapy for advanced or metastatic disease.

Patients with ES-SCLC and disease progression on or after standard of care (SoC). For dose expansion only: no more than 2 prior lines of therapy for advanced or metastatic disease are allowed.

Phase II:

HR+/HER2- aBC with disease progression on an aromatase inhibitor or tamoxifen in combination with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for unresectable/metastatic disease with no more than 2 lines of endocrine therapy.

Measurable disease as determined by RECIST v1.1.

BC only: If no measurable disease is present, then at least one predominantly lytic bone lesion must be present that can be accurately assessed at baseline and is suitable for repeated assessment.

Exclusion Criteria:

Previous treatment with a CDK2 inhibitor at any time.

Patients with inadequate bone marrow and/or organ functions with out-of-range laboratory values.

Clinically significant, uncontrolled heart disease and/or cardiac repolarization abnormality including MI, CABG, long QT syndrome, or risk factors for TdP.

Presence of symptomatic CNS metastases or CNS metastases that require local therapy or increasing doses of corticosteroids within 2 weeks prior to study entry.

For the combination treatment:

Patients with symptomatic visceral disease or any disease burden that makes the patient ineligible for endocrine-based therapy.

Patients who could not tolerate the prescribed dose of ribociclib during a previous course of treatment, requiring dose reduction or permanent discontinuation due to adverse events.

For patients with BC: Patient is concurrently using hormone replacement therapy.

WOCBP who are unwilling to use highly effective contraception methods, pregnant or nursing women.

Some communication breakdowns lead to adverse events and even harmful errors. Deficiencies in provider-patient communication can compound patients' distress, lower the quality of care, and disrupt patient-provider relationships. There is little research on patients' and providers' experiences of the communication breakdowns that precipitate adverse events and errors, or on effective responses to these events. Because of this, cancer providers are unsure how to communicate with patients in these difficult situations. The goal of the proposed study is to improve patient-centered communication around adverse events and errors in cancer care. Our specific aims are: 1) To describe patients' experiences with communication around adverse events and errors in cancer care, 2) To describe providers' experiences and practices with communication around adverse events and errors in cancer care, 3) To develop practical recommendations, provider training materials and patient educational materials for improving communication around adverse events and errors in cancer care, 4) To disseminate the recommendations and materials through three health plans, and 5) To conduct a preliminary evaluation of the perceived usefulness and impact of the materials. The investigators will first conduct interviews with breast and colorectal cancer patients who have experienced adverse events or errors at 3 Cancer Research Network (CRN) health plans (Atlanta, Georgia; Seattle, Washington and Worcester, Massachusetts). The interviews will focus on instances where patients believe that better communication might have prevented an adverse event or error, or mitigated the event's impact. Next the investigators will conduct focus groups to understand providers' attitudes and experiences with these communication dilemmas, and use simulations to describe providers' communication practices. Finally, the investigators will interview health plan leaders to identify the systems factors that influence communication with patients around adverse events and errors. These perspectives will be synthesized to create patient and provider educational material for improving communication. Three advisory panels: a Patient Advisory Panel, a Health Plan Advisory Panel and a Dissemination Advisory Panel (including all 14 CRN health plans) will help create and disseminate these educational interventions. Dissemination will occur at the three core clinical sites. The investigators use patient and provider surveys to evaluate the educational materials' impact. This evaluation will provide the evidence-base to refine the study products before widespread dissemination throughout the CRN and beyond. XL418 is a new chemical entity that inhibits a spectrum of targets, including Akt and p70S6K, that mediate PI3 Kinase / PTEN signaling."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Cancer","Solid Tumors"],"keywords":["Cancer","Solid Tumors"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["PHASE1"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"NON_RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"SINGLE_GROUP","primaryPurpose":"TREATMENT","maskingInfo":{"masking":"NONE"}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":63,"type":"ESTIMATED"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"interventions":[{"type":"DRUG","name":"XL418"}]},"outcomesModule":{"primaryOutcomes":[{"measure":"Safety, tolerability, and maximum tolerated dose of XL418 with daily oral administration"}],"secondaryOutcomes":[{"measure":"Plasma pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamic effects of daily oral administration of XL418"}]},"eligibilityModule":{"eligibilityCriteria":"Inclusion Criteria:

1. The subject has a histologically confirmed solid tumor that is metastatic or unresectable, for which standard curative or palliative measures do not exist or are no longer effective, and there are no known therapies to prolong survival.
2. The subject has disease that is assessable by tumor marker, physical, or radiologic means.
3. The subject is ≥18 years old.
4. The subject's weight is ≥55 kg and ≤120 kg.
5. The subject has an ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) performance status ≤2.
6. The subject has adequate organ and marrow function.
7. For subjects who are to be enrolled into the expanded MTD cohort:

   1. tumor tissue amenable to serial biopsy; and
   2. additional informed consent.
8. The subject is capable of understanding the protocol and has signed the informed consent document.
9. Sexually active subjects (male and female) must use medically acceptable methods of contraception during the course of the study.
10. Female subjects of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test at screening.
11. The subject has a normal fasting blood glucose level at screening.
12. If a subject has received more than three prior regimens of cytotoxic chemotherapy, more than two biological regimens, or more than 3000 cGy to areas containing substantial marrow, the principal investigator (PI) and the sponsor will discuss subject suitability prior to enrollment.
13. The subject has had no other diagnosis of malignancy (unless non-melanoma skin cancer, in situ carcinoma of the cervix, or a malignancy diagnosed ≥5 years ago, with no evidence of disease for 5 years prior to screening for this study).

Exclusion Criteria:

1. The subject has received anticancer treatment (eg, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, cytokines, or hormones) within 30 days (6 weeks for nitrosoureas or mitomycin C) before the first dose of study drug.
2. The subject has received radiation to ≥25% of his or her bone marrow within 30 days of treatment with XL418.

Giving more than one drug may kill more tumor cells.

PURPOSE: This phase II trial is studying how well giving irinotecan together with carboplatin as upfront window therapy (first-line therapy) works in treating patients with newly diagnosed intermediate-risk or high-risk rhabdomyosarcoma.","detailedDescription":"OBJECTIVES:

Primary

* Determine the response rate in patients with newly diagnosed intermediate- or high-risk rhabdomyosarcoma treated with upfront window therapy comprising irinotecan and carboplatin.
* Determine the acute toxic effects of this regimen combined with radiotherapy in these patients.
* Determine the safety and feasibility of this regimen in these patients.
* Determine the rate of local control achieved in patients treated with this regimen in combination with intensity-modulated radiotherapy.
* Determine the safety and feasibility of administering maintenance therapy comprising irinotecan to patients with high-risk rhabdomyosarcoma treated with this regimen.

Secondary

* Correlate, preliminarily, in vitro measurements of angiogenesis with clinical features (extent of disease), response to therapy, and outcome in patients treated with this regimen.
* Determine, preliminarily, the efficacy of this regimen, in terms of improved outcomes, in these patients.

OUTLINE: This is a pilot study.

* Courses 1 and 2: Patients receive carboplatin IV over 1 hour on day 1 and irinotecan IV over 1 hour on days 1-5 and 8-12. Treatment repeats every 21 days for a total of 2 courses.
* Courses 3-5: Patients receive vincristine IV on days 1, 8, and 15; dexrazoxane IV over 15-30 minutes, doxorubicin IV over 15-30 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1 and 2; and filgrastim (G-CSF) subcutaneously (SC) once daily beginning on approximately day 3 and continuing until blood counts recover. Treatment repeats every 21 days for a total of 3 courses.

Some patients may undergo surgical resection of the tumor after completion of course 5. After course 5, patients undergo radiotherapy once daily, 5 days a week, for 4-5.5 weeks.

* Courses 6 and 7\*: Patients receive vincristine IV and carboplatin IV over 1 hour on day 1; irinotecan IV over 1 hour on days 1-5 and 8-12; and G-CSF SC once daily beginning on approximately day 13 and continuing until blood counts recover. Treatment repeats every 21 days for a total of 2 courses.

NOTE: \*Patients who develop disease progression during courses 1 or 2 do not receive further irinotecan and carboplatin. Instead, patients receive ifosfamide and etoposide as in courses 8 and 9.

* Courses 8 and 9: Patients receive vincristine IV on day 1; etoposide IV over 1 hour and ifosfamide IV over 2 hours on days 1-5; and G-CSF SC once daily beginning on approximately day 6 and continuing until blood counts recover. Treatment repeats every 21 days for a total of 2 courses.
* Course 10: Patients receive vincristine IV on days 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 36, and 43; dexrazoxane IV over 15-30 minutes, doxorubicin IV over 15-30 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1 and 2; and filgrastim SC beginning on approximately day 3 and continuing until blood counts recover (1 course).
* Course 11 and 12: Patients receive etoposide IV over 1 hour and ifosfamide IV over 2 hours on days 1-5 and G-CSF SC once daily beginning on approximately day 6 and continuing until blood counts recover. Treatment repeats every 21 days for a total of 2 courses.

Patients with high-risk disease proceed to maintenance therapy.

* Maintenance therapy\*: Patients receive irinotecan IV over 1 hour on days 1-5 and 8-12. Treatment repeats every 21 days for a total of 6 courses.

NOTE: \*Patients who develop disease progression during courses 1 or 2 do not receive further irinotecan.

In all courses, treatment continues in the absence of unacceptable toxicity or disease progression or recurrence after initial response.

Patients are followed monthly for 1 year, every 3 months for 1 year, every 6 months for 1 year, and then annually thereafter.

\*Starting with A(8), patients will undergo PET Scans instead of Bone Scans, at the discretion of the PI."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Sarcoma"],"keywords":["previously untreated childhood How well the lymphoma responds to the initial 3 doses of tislelizumab","detailedDescription":"Trial patients who are deemed eligible for the trial will receive 3 cycles of tislelizumab which will be administered at a dose of 200 mg (IV) on day 1 of each 21-day cycle. Patients with early stage lymphoma and no high-risk features who respond very well to the initial 3 doses of tislelizumab will receive a further 2 doses of tislelizumab, followed by radiotherapy, followed by tislelizumab once every 21 days for up to 2 years.

All other patients will receive a combination of tislelizumab with chemotherapy for between 2 and 6 cycles. Each cycle will last 28 days. Tislelizumab will be given on day 1 and chemotherapy (doxorubicin (also known as Adriamycin), vinblastine and dacarbazine, or AVD) will be given on days 1 and 15, as injections or infusions into a vein. Following this some patients may require radiotherapy depending on their response to treatment.

Patients who are in complete metabolic response (CMR) at PET1 will receive 2 fewer cycles of tislelizumab and AVD therapy than those not in CMR.

A further 1 or 2 PET scans will be performed to assess how well the lymphoma has responded to the trial treatment, depending on the results of previous scans. After completing the treatment patients will then be followed-up for at least 2 years from the start of their participation in the trial.

Note: Initial patients will be recruited to a safety run in. 2. Age 60 years or over
3. In the view of the investigator, fit for combination chemotherapy (includes those who would require planned dose reduction although no lower than 50% doxorubicin)
4. Written informed consent
5. Measurable disease on contrast enhanced CT as defined by Cheson et al., 2014 1 (Nodal lesion of longest diameter 1.5 cm or extranodal lesion of longest diameter 1.0 cm).
6. ECOG performance status 0-2
7. Adequate bone marrow function (Platelets ≥ 75 x 109/L without platelet transfusion for 72 hours, Neutrophils ≥ 1.0 x 109/L without G-CSF for 7 days)
8. Adequate liver function tests (ALT / AST ≤ 2.5 x ULN, total serum bilirubin ≤ 1.5 x ULN)
9. Creatinine Clearance ≥ 30 ml/min as defined by the Cockroft-Gault equation
10. Adequate cardiac function as determined by a transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrating left ventricular ejection fraction is ≥ 50% and confirming the absence of severe valvular heart disease
11. Willing to comply with the contraceptive requirements of the trial
12. Willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment plan, laboratory tests and other study procedures

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma
2. History of autoimmune disorders (with the exception of hypothyroidism, type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, alopecia)
3. History of solid organ transplant
4. Grade 2 or higher peripheral neuropathy
5. Presentation with disease causing symptomatic compression of vital structures (e.g. stridor due to tracheal compression). Other cases of radiological compression of vital structures require discussion with TMG prior to registration
6. Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding
7. Active hepatitis B or C infection defined by

   1. Hepatitis B surface antigen positivity OR
   2. Anti-hepatitis B core antibody positivity with detectable circulating HBV DNA (hepatitis B core antibody patients with undetectable circulating HBV DNA are eligible but must take suitable prophylaxis for reactivation)
   3. Anti-Hepatitis C antibody positivity unless patient has been treated for hepatitis C and has undetectable HCV RNA
8. Known HIV infection
9. Positive PCR for SAR-CoV-2 RNA within the 2 weeks prior to registration. Patients with a history of SARS-CoV-2 are required to have a documented negative PCR swab since documented SARS-CoV-2 infection
10. Immunosuppressive therapy within the 2 months prior to registration apart from inhaled, intranasal or topical corticosteroids. Systemic corticosteroids are permitted prior to study entry but must be weaned to 10 mg prednisolone / day for a minimum of 7 days prior to cycle 1 day 1
11. Live vaccine given within 30 days prior to registration
12. Active infection requiring systemic therapy with ongoing symptoms at registration or where the planned duration of therapy would continue beyond cycle 1 day 1
13. Major surgery within 4 weeks prior to registration (excisional biopsy is not considered major surgery)
14. Myocardial infarction, unstable angina, coronary artery bypass graft, cerebrovascular accident or transient ischaemic attack within 6 months prior to registration
15. Previously treated haematological malignancy
16. Solid-organ malignancy active within the last 3 years, except where the natural history or treatment does not have the potential to interfere with assessment of safety or efficacy of trial treatment, for example:

    1. Adequately treated non-melanoma skin cancer considered to be in remission
    2. Melanoma in situ following resection
    3. Carcinoma in situ of the breast or cervix
    4. Carcinoma of the prostate of Gleason grade 6 or less with stable prostate-specific antigen levels
    5. Cancer considered cured by surgical resection or unlikely to impact survival in the next 3 years, for example local transitional carcinoma of the bladder or benign tumours of the adrenal gland or pancreas
17. A history of other malignancies should be discussed with the trial management group prior to registration

studies the side effects and best dose of ipilimumab when given after chemoradiation therapy in treating patients with stages IB2-IIB or IIIB-IVA cervical cancer. Drugs used in chemotherapy, such as cisplatin, work in different ways to stop the growth of tumor cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing, or by stopping them from spreading. Radiation therapy uses high-energy x-rays to kill tumor cells and shrink tumors. Monoclonal antibodies, such as ipilimumab, may find tumor cells and help carry tumor-killing substances to them. Giving ipilimumab together with chemoradiation therapy may be a better way treat cervical cancer.","detailedDescription":"PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To estimate the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) of adjuvant ipilimumab following concurrent weekly cisplatin and extended field radiation in women with newly diagnosed locally advanced cervical cancer stage IB2/ IIA with-positive para-aortic lymph nodes only and stage IIB/IIIB/IVA with positive lymph nodes.

II. To determine the feasibility of the treatment regimen over the four cycles of adjuvant ipilimumab once the MTD is estimated.

III. To assess the toxicities of the treatment regimen per the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 4.0.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To examine progression free survival for 1 year after study completion. II. To determine site of recurrence, loco-regional versus distant, for one year after completion of therapy.

III. To estimate the frequency of chronic toxicities experienced within one year after completion of therapy.

TERTIARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To enumerate the human papillomavirus (HPV)-subtype-specific T-cells and characterize the kinetics of HPV-subtype-specific T-cell expansion associated with chemoradiation and ipilimumab treatment.

II. To characterize the association between differential expression of immune markers on leukocytes from human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-A\*0201 patients and response to chemoradiation and ipilimumab treatment.

Typical reported exercise barriers are inconvenient location (e.g. long distance from home), exercise at an unfavorable time of the day, inadequate access to cancer-specific exercise and insufficient recommendations from healthcare providers. Thus, there is need for more research on resistance exercise with an alternative approach in cancer rehabilitation, that potentially can target a broad range of patients, despite their domicile. In Norway, the foundation "Active against cancer" has established exercise locations targeting cancer patients in several hospitals, and today they also offer digital home-based exercise sessions. Therefore, the overall research objectives are to compare the efficacy of a 12 weeks digital, home-based resistance exercise program for cancer patients after treatment on functional, mental, and metabolic health, compared to the same program conducted in a studio under guidance of an instructor. The primary aim is to compare the effect on exercise adherence between digital home-based exercise program and the on-site guided program in cancer patients after treatment. Secondary aims are to compare the two groups on several functional health outcomes, mental health outcomes and metabolic health markers.
